item.title: The geopolitical stakes of AI: Why leaders must watch the sovereign AI race
item.description:
AI has evolved past simple corporate optimization. Today, it is a definitive engine of macroeconomic power. All over the world, governments and large corporations are launching highly subsidized efforts to develop their own artificial intelligence. For C-level executives, this shift signals a fundamental reorganization of the global tech stack. The decisions made by global superpowers today will directly impact supply chains, compliance requirements, and data architectures tomorrow.

According to researchers at Bain & Company, governments worldwide—including India, Japan, France, Canada, and the United Arab Emirates—are spending billions of dollars to subsidize sovereign AI. They are investing heavily in domestic computing infrastructure and localized AI models trained on regional data and native languages. Market intelligence from McKinsey & Company estimates that sovereign AI could represent a market of $600 billion by 2030. Furthermore, a survey of executives, investors, and government offices revealed that 71% believe sovereign AI is an “existential concern” or “strategic imperative” for their organizational goals.

For CIOs and CTOs, understanding the underlying drivers of this movement is essential for future-proofing corporate IT strategy. Below are the core factors forcing global leaders to act, along with the strategic trade-offs every organization must consider.

The core drivers of the sovereign AI movement:

  • Economic competition and zero-sum dynamics: The economic implications of the AI race mirror the early days of the commercial internet, but at an accelerated velocity. Research published by the McKinsey Global Institute suggests that generative AI could generate as much as $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion in annual economic value alone. In this highly volatile geopolitical landscape, multilateral collaboration is surrendering to unilateral competition. AI has become the premier battlefield for nations competing for economic leadership, turning the technological landscape into a zero-sum game.
  • National security and infrastructure resilience: Digital sovereignty policies are increasingly serving as a bulwark for security. If foundational AI models become the primary engine of a nation’s economy, depending on foreign cloud providers or cross-border infrastructure introduces a vulnerability. An adversary could cause catastrophic disruption simply by knocking those external capabilities offline. Consequently, state leaders are highly hesitant to trust foreign entities—even close geopolitical allies—with such critical infrastructure assets.
  • Data governance and local values: Training enterprise-grade models requires immense data volumes, which many governments view as an intrinsic risk to data privacy and regulatory alignment. By building local sovereign infrastructure, nations can institute precise governance controls to protect rights and uphold regional laws. Beyond regulatory compliance, leaders are prioritizing AI systems that accurately reflect and shape the specific societies they serve, so local languages, historical nuances, and distinct ethical values are deeply embedded in the underlying models.

Navigating the corporate impact: Trade-offs for the C-suite

As nations build localized tech stacks, enterprise leadership teams face complex trade-offs regarding vendor lock-in, data hosting, and infrastructure costs. Research firm Gartner says that nations establishing a sovereign AI stack will need to invest at least 1% of their GDP in AI infrastructure by 2029. Enterprise leaders must balance the benefits of public cloud scalability against the compliance of regionalized hardware.

  • Security vs. flexibility: Standardizing on a single, global public cloud provider maximizes engineering speed. However, it exposes the business to regulatory penalties or abrupt service disruptions if international data laws shift.
  • Local compliance vs. operational scale: Deploying sovereign infrastructure can provide compliance with regional governance laws. Yet, managing isolated data silos across multiple countries increases operational complexity and drives up total cost of ownership (TCO).

Strategic recommendations for CIOs

To prepare for an increasingly fractured and regionalized tech ecosystem, executive leadership teams should prioritize two immediate actions:

  1. Audit infrastructure interdependencies: Evaluate your current vendor portfolio to identify dependencies on centralized cloud ecosystems. Begin mapping how a sudden shift toward nationalized data borders would impact your analytics and operational models.
  2. Evaluate strategic supercomputing partners: When planning long-term AI architecture, align with technology suppliers who possess a verified track record of building large-scale supercomputers and enterprise-grade data factories. AI data center solutions require intentional hardware and public-sector expertise to maintain resilience.

The enterprise tech stack is no longer decoupled from global politics. To understand how these national investments will transform corporate AI deployment, security standards, and infrastructure requirements, read The race is on: 6 reasons why countries are rushing to develop sovereign AI.

*************

HPE and AMD are partnering to deliver the next generation of AI and supercomputing infrastructure. Combining HPE’s deep expertise in large-scale system design with AMD EPYC™ processors and AMD Instinct™ accelerators, the two companies help customers build platforms capable of supporting the most demanding AI, modeling, simulation, and analytics workloads. Whether accelerating scientific research, enabling digital engineering, or training advanced AI models, HPE and AMD focus on what matters most: faster insights, greater efficiency, and the flexibility to scale. Together, they provide the technology foundation organizations need to solve complex problems, drive discovery, and create lasting business and societal impact.

item.title: The open compute revolution: Why the C-suite is redefining the modern data center
item.description:
For years, the enterprise data center operated under a predictable, if restrictive, playbook. Siloed, proprietary hardware stacks dictated infrastructure life cycles, leaving CIOs locked into vendor ecosystems. Every hardware refresh meant navigating premium pricing, constrained supply chains, and artificial limitations on interoperability.

Today, that playbook is being rewritten. As AI, massive data analytics, and intense computational demands reshape corporate strategies, C-level executives are turning to Open Compute infrastructure. Originally pioneered by hyperscalers to manage massive scale efficiently, open hardware design has graduated to the enterprise. By decoupling software from proprietary hardware and embracing collaborative, community-driven standards, open compute is no longer just a technical preference—it is a strategic business imperative.

For the C-suite, transitioning to an open infrastructure model solves three critical pain points: accelerating technological agility, optimizing total cost of ownership (TCO), and meeting aggressive corporate sustainability targets.

Here are the three primary reasons why open compute infrastructure has become vital for IT strategy, and how leaders like HPE and AMD are making it more accessible for the enterprise.

1. Shattering vendor lock-in to accelerate enterprise agility

In a rapidly shifting market, operational agility is a primary competitive advantage. Traditional, proprietary data center architectures restrict a company’s ability to pivot. If a specific vendor faces supply chain disruptions or falls behind in processing power, the enterprise suffers.

Open Compute infrastructure dismantles these artificial barriers. By adhering to open-source hardware specifications, enterprises gain the freedom to mix, match, and upgrade components without replacing their entire infrastructure. This modularity means that hardware can keep pace with software innovations.

This is where the collaboration between hardware pioneers becomes essential. HPE has championed this shift by bringing enterprise-grade reliability, support, and life cycle management to open, flexible architectures. Rather than forcing companies into closed systems, HPE delivers the scaling benefits of open design backed by global service-level agreements (SLAs). For the C-suite, this means the flexibility of an open ecosystem without the operational risk of managing unverified white-box hardware.

2. Optimizing total cost of ownership (TCO) at scale

Inflationary pressures and flat IT budgets mean CFOs are scrutinizing capital expenditures (CapEx) and operating expenses (OpEx) more closely than ever. Closed, proprietary systems carry a premium—not just in the initial purchase price, but in specialized maintenance, proprietary cables, and restricted upgrade paths.

Open Compute infrastructure fundamentally alters data center economics in three distinct ways:

  • Component standardization: Standardized form factors reduce the cost of spare parts and simplify physical deployment.
  • Streamlined maintenance: Stripping away cosmetic bezels and redundant, proprietary management tools allows IT teams to service systems faster.
  • Extended life cycles: Instead of replacing an entire server chassis, executives can upgrade individual components, such as upgrading processors while retaining the existing racks and power distribution units.

Powering these cost-effective, high-density environments requires a new standard in silicon efficiency. AMD has been central to this economic shift. By delivering high-core-density processors like AMD EPYC™, they allow enterprises to consolidate their physical footprint. Fewer sockets mean lower software licensing fees and reduced hardware costs, directly translating to optimized TCO that keeps financial officers satisfied.

3. Driving meaningful progress toward sustainability goals

Data centers are among the world’s most energy-intensive facilities, making them a primary target for corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics. For CEOs and chief sustainability officers, reducing carbon footprints is no longer an afterthought—it is a board-level mandate. Some traditional servers include inefficient power supplies and restrictive airflow designs that can drive up cooling costs.

Open Compute architectures tackle energy consumption from the ground up. By utilizing centralized, highly efficient rack-level power distribution and optimizing physical layouts for improved airflow, open designs can reduce Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) ratios.

When you pair open-rack efficiency with energy-efficient silicon, the sustainability gains multiply. AMD’s continuous focus on performance-per-watt efficiency enables data centers to handle exponentially more compute volume without a corresponding spike in energy consumption. This combination allows enterprise leaders to scale their compute capabilities to handle more intense workloads while visibly driving down operational emissions and meeting corporate sustainability milestones.

The C-suite verdict: Future-proofing the enterprise

Open Compute infrastructure is no longer an experimental architecture reserved solely for hyperscale tech giants. Through enterprise-ready offerings from trusted partners like HPE and cutting-edge silicon from AMD, open infrastructure has become a practical, scalable option for mainstream corporations.

For C-level executives, the decision to migrate toward open standards represents a fundamental commitment to the future. It provides the financial relief required by the CFO, the sustainability metrics demanded by the CEO, and the technological agility needed by the CIO to lead the enterprise into the future.

Three quick tips for C-level executives getting started with Open Compute

  • Audit current refresh cycles: Identify proprietary hardware due for replacement over the next 18 months and map out Open-Compute alternatives to benchmark TCO improvements.
  • Prioritize workload density over raw hardware volume: Partner with architecture leaders like HPE and AMD to design high-core-density configurations that slash operational footprint and licensing overhead.
  • Align infrastructure updates with sustainability reporting timelines: Measure the energy-efficiency gains of moving to centralized power and highly efficient processors to demonstrate tangible carbon reductions to shareholders.

Shape the future of infrastructure: Join the Open Compute community

True innovation doesn’t happen in isolation. The power of Open Compute lies in its global community of engineering experts, visionary developers, and enterprise leaders who collaborate to solve the industry’s toughest data center challenges. By actively participating in the Open Compute Project (OCP), your organization can help define next-generation specifications, preview upcoming silicon and server road maps, and share deployment best practices alongside industry pioneers like HPE and AMD.

Don’t just adapt to the future—help build it. Visit the official Open Compute Project website today to explore active project groups, attend upcoming regional summits, and discover how your enterprise can contribute to a more efficient, collaborative, and sustainable technological landscape.

Together, they provide the technology foundation organizations need to solve complex problems, drive discovery, and create lasting business and societal impact.

item.title: The sovereign AI mandate: How Germany’s HLRS is anchoring Europe’s digital future
item.description:
As organizations scale out their production AI infrastructure, technology leaders are moving from localized model optimization to the more complex realities of industrial-grade deployment. For those who have spent years embedding machine learning into their core business processes, the current inflection point is defined by massive data pipelines, expanding compute clusters, and strict data governance. Scaling out requires an architectural evaluation: Can your infrastructure support exponential workload growth while simultaneously keeping your data entirely secure and compliant?

For European CIOs and engineering teams tasked with managing this operational expansion, scaling introduces a critical structural bottleneck: Where does our data live at scale, and who ultimately controls the underlying infrastructure?

In an era of intensive model training and widespread inference deployment, relying blindly on public cloud environments presents significant long-term structural risks. For organizations operating under stringent local regulations like the EU AI Act, expanding your AI footprint means managing larger volumes of proprietary intellectual property and customer data than ever before. If that scaling happens across jurisdictions that do not align with European privacy laws, your entire competitive advantage and regulatory standing could be compromised.

This clear need for scalable, autonomous infrastructure has catalyzed a major movement across the continent: Sovereign AI. At the absolute center of this infrastructure paradigm shift is the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart (HLRS) in Germany. As an elite computing institution, HLRS is serving as the operational blueprint for how European enterprises can aggressively scale out their AI implementations without sacrificing absolute data sovereignty.

The modern enterprise challenge: Innovation vs. autonomy

For years, commercial enterprises looking to train massive AI models had few choices outside the major global hyperscale cloud providers. While these platforms offered rapid scalability, they also created a complex web of dependencies. European enterprises frequently encountered architectural lock-in, unpredictable data egress fees, and the persistent compliance headache of transferring sensitive data across international borders.

For organizations in highly regulated sectors—such as automotive engineering, financial services, aerospace, and healthcare—these barriers were often insurmountable. Innovation slowed because the risk of exposing proprietary data was simply too high.

HLRS recognized this friction point early on. Rather than forcing organizations to compromise between computational horsepower and data security, the center designed an environment specifically tailored to the unique operational, cultural, and legal realities of European industry.

A deeply customer-centric approach to high-performance computing

HLRS does not view itself merely as a data center filled with flashing server racks; it operates as a specialized co-innovation partner for industrial enterprises and scientific researchers.

HLRS provides a unique collaborative bridge between academic research and commercial application. Its customer-centric model enables an industrial engineering team or a climate research group to receive tailored computational environments optimized for their specific mathematical models and workflows.

Consider the automotive industry, a cornerstone of the German economy. Designing the next generation of autonomous or electric vehicles requires running billions of simulation cycles. By leveraging the local, highly secure infrastructure at HLRS, these manufacturers can train complex AI vision models and run aerodynamic simulations knowing that their intellectual property remains fully insulated from external entities. The data stays in Germany, conforms entirely to European standards, yet benefits from processing speeds that rival supercomputing clusters around the world.

This customer-first focus democratizes access to elite computing. It allows midsize enterprises and massive multinational corporations alike to scale their AI ambitions without the fear of compromising their foundational data assets.

Engineering sovereign AI: The powerhouse ecosystem

Building a sovereign computing ecosystem capable of supporting next-generation AI workloads requires an extraordinary combination of hardware reliability, system architecture, and processing efficiency. To deliver this level of performance to its users, HLRS has cultivated deep strategic partnerships with industry-leading technology pioneers including HPE and AMD.

1. Architecting the future

AI and deep learning workloads are fundamentally different from traditional corporate computing. They require massive data pipelines to move fluidly across thousands of nodes without encountering bottlenecks. HPE brings its world-class supercomputing system architecture to the HLRS data center floor.

By utilizing HPE Cray Supercomputing platforms, HLRS can offer its users an infrastructure optimized for massive parallel processing. HPE advanced liquid-cooling technologies help maximize data center energy efficiency—a critical requirement for European organizations operating under sustainability mandates. For the HLRS customer, this translates to predictable, highly reliable performance even when training the most demanding, multibillion-parameter AI models.

2. Driving computational breakthroughs

Today’s AI workloads are incredibly compute-intensive, requiring advanced hardware capable of executing complex matrix mathematics at blinding speeds. HLRS integrates cutting-edge AMD processors and accelerators to meet these heavy operational demands.

AMD-powered infrastructure is deliberately engineered to handle both traditional high-performance computing simulations and modern AI training workloads simultaneously. Plus, AMD’s focus on energy efficiency per watt allows HLRS to maximize its computational output without exponentially increasing its environmental footprint. For end users, this means faster time-to-insight, accelerated product development cycles, and the ability to iterate on AI models at a fraction of the time.

By tightly integrating HPE system engineering with AMD processing innovation, HLRS delivers a sovereign computing alternative that matches—and often exceeds—the capabilities of non-sovereign platforms.

The strategic value for the enterprise CIO

For CIOs, the lesson of the HLRS model is clear: sovereign AI is no longer a niche regulatory preference; it is a core business strategy. Investing in sovereign architectures allows organizations to achieve three critical enterprise goals:

  • Future-proof compliance: By anchoring AI development within a sovereign framework, organizations can be insulated from shifting international compliance regulations and the evolving complexities of global data laws.
  • Intellectual property protection: Keeping model training local means proprietary algorithms, customer data, and trade secrets don’t feed into public or third-party AI models.
  • Uncompromised performance: Selecting a dedicated infrastructure stack powered by HPE and AMD enables local data processing without sacrificing the speed or scale required to compete on a global stage.

As AI continues to mature, the organizations that build their digital strategies on a foundation of data autonomy and sovereignty will be the ones positioned to lead. HLRS stands as a powerful testament to what is possible when customer-focused design meets world-class technology infrastructure.

Learn more about Europe’s strategic investments in digital autonomy, the evolution of supercomputing, and how industrial organizations are leveraging these advanced technologies to drive competitive advantage by listening to the full conversation on This Week in HPC Podcast Episode 400.

item.title: The unit of scale is not headcount
item.description:
Every platform leader I know is being asked the same question: How do you deliver more with less?

The usual answers are familiar: hire more people, add more process or ask the existing team to move faster.

All three miss the underlying constraint. Headcount is an input. Throughput is an outcome. Organizational complexity is a cost.

Adding people can increase capacity, but it also adds communication paths, onboarding, coordination and decision overhead. Adding process can create consistency, but it can also slow the decisions it was meant to improve. Asking a team to work harder eventually consumes the very capacity you are trying to increase.

There is another answer: design the organization so ownership scales faster than headcount. That means deliberately small pods with sharp charters, end-to-end ownership and aggressive use of automation, platforms and AI.

I spent more than a decade running provisioning and lifecycle for very large infrastructure fleets at VMware, where small teams operated systems at a scale that looked impossible on paper. Today I lead an engineering organization of three teams at Stripe, built from a half dozen pods, each with its own charter and a large scope that nests into the team and organization charters above it. The lesson has held in both environments: the unit of scale isn’t headcount. It’s ownership.

Small pods work because they concentrate ownership, reduce coordination and make leverage compound.

The headcount trap

When a leader says they need more people, they usually mean they need more throughput. The two are not the same.

Brooks made this point in The Mythical Man-Month: adding people to a late project can make it later because communication paths grow faster than headcount. The tax does not stop at communication. Every additional person can add onboarding, alignment, decision-making, context sharing and ownership ambiguity. As organizations grow, nobody can hold the entire problem in their head. The organization compensates with meetings, documentation, processes and coordination roles.

You haven’t necessarily bought capacity. You may have bought complexity.

This does not mean hiring is bad. Growing teams and increasing scope often require more people. The mistake is treating headcount as the default answer to every capacity problem.

Before adding people, ask a harder question: What is preventing the existing people from owning more?

Sometimes the answer is genuinely capacity. Often, it is handoffs, fragmented ownership, repetitive work, unclear boundaries or systems that nobody has permission to retire. Those are organizational design problems.

The squeeze-harder response fails differently but just as predictably. The engineers who absorb extra load quietly are usually your strongest ones. They are also the ones with the most options elsewhere. You won’t see the organizational cost immediately. You’ll see it when they leave.

Design for ownership

A pod is a small group of engineers with one clear charter and ownership of a meaningful scope from end to end: building it, operating it and eventually retiring it.

The exact number matters less than the principle. The group should be small enough that its members can understand the problem, make decisions without extensive coordination, and maintain unambiguous ownership. The goal isn’t to hit a magic headcount. It is to keep the cognitive and coordination load low enough that ownership remains clear.

The charter is what makes that possible. A good charter is one sentence that names what the pod owns and, just as importantly, what it does not.

“Own the lifecycle of this fleet, end to end” is a charter.
 “Help with infrastructure” is a wish.

In my organization, each pod’s charter is large in scope but sharp at the edges. Pod charters roll up into team charters, and team charters roll up into the organization charter. That hierarchy creates something more valuable than organizational neatness: decision rights.

When a request arrives that fits no charter, it becomes a visible leadership decision. Should we create a new pod? Change an existing charter? Stop doing something else? Or explicitly decline the work?

Without clear boundaries, the same request usually finds the most helpful engineer and becomes someone’s spare-time responsibility. That is how organizational entropy starts.

End-to-end ownership is the real multiplier. When the same people who build a system operate it and eventually decommission it, handoffs disappear. Waiting disappears with them. Quality improves because the people creating the system are also responsible for living with its consequences. Decisions get faster because there is no ambiguity about who gets to make them.

Ownership compresses organizational latency.

The leverage stack

Small pods only outperform if human effort is multiplied. A three-person pod delivering ten-person impact isn’t doing ten people’s work through heroics. It is using leverage.

I think about that leverage in three forms: automation, shared platforms and AI.

Automation

The first form is automation. I have run one rule for years: a repeated task is a bug in the system, not a job description.

If a pod does something twice by hand, the third time it should become code, a pipeline or a paved path that makes the right way the easy way. The system should do the repetitive work. Humans should do the judgment work.

Platforms

The second form is organizational leverage. Shared platforms, paved roads, reusable infrastructure and common capabilities allow every pod to build on work that someone else has already done. A pod that can consume a reliable internal platform ships like a team much larger than itself. A pod that has to build its own foundations is a small team doing a large team’s plumbing.

The best platform work therefore does more than improve one team’s productivity. It multiplies the capacity of every team that depends on it.

AI

The third form is increasingly AI. The interesting question isn’t whether an engineer can write code faster with AI. The more important question is whether AI allows a pod to absorb more scope without adding people by reducing the cost of cognitive work.

AI can help pods investigate unfamiliar systems, generate and analyze code, create tests and documentation, accelerate onboarding and absorb routine operational work. That creates a new kind of leverage: compressing work that previously consumed significant engineering time.

But AI does not fix organizational ambiguity. It amplifies the structure it lands in. A pod with a sharp charter, clean interfaces and strong ownership can turn AI into leverage. A vague organization with an AI assistant can simply produce ambiguity faster.

The goal isn’t AI-powered productivity for its own sake. The goal is increasing the scope a team can responsibly own.

The hardest decision is what not to do

None of this is free. Staying small requires decisions that often feel wrong in the moment.

The first is choosing what not to staff. Every planning cycle produces more good ideas than the organization has capacity to pursue. The design only holds if you let some of those ideas die on the table. A pod at 120% of its charter is not a success story. It is a slow failure with good PR.

The second is allowing pods to kill their own systems. End-to-end ownership includes the end. A pod that cannot retire its own work accumulates systems faster than it can eliminate them. Eventually, engineers spend more capacity feeding old systems than creating new value. Some of the highest leverage work my teams have done has been turning things off.

The third is saying no to good ideas because the pod is full. Not “not yet.” Not “let’s find a way.” No. The charter is the reason. It feels harsh. What is actually harsh is saying yes and allowing the pod to discover the cost at 2 a.m.

The hardest part of small-pod design is not deciding what each pod should do. It is deciding what the organization will deliberately not do. That is a leadership responsibility.

Defend the boundary

The biggest threat to a small pod isn’t failure. It is success.

Successful teams attract scope. A team solves one problem, so someone asks it to solve the adjacent problem. Another stakeholder has a one-off request. A system loses its owner and suddenly the successful team becomes the obvious new home for it.

None of these requests is unreasonable individually. Together, they create organizational entropy. A successful pod can quietly become the large, overloaded team it was designed to replace.

Defending small is therefore active work.

The charter is the first line of defense. Requests outside it get a visible decision, not quiet absorption.

The second is regularly reviewing what each pod is actually carrying against what its charter says. Scope drift is much easier to see on paper than in someone’s calendar.

The third is recognizing when a pod has genuinely outgrown its design. When a pod’s scope has legitimately doubled and stayed there, the answer isn’t to quietly double the size of the pod. Split the scope. Create two pods with two clear charters.

Scale the ownership boundary, not the coordination burden.

When small pods don’t work

Small pods are not a universal answer.

Some problems genuinely require larger groups or tightly coupled expertise. Some domains have operational, security, regulatory or reliability requirements that make a very small team impractical. Some work is inherently exploratory and doesn’t yet have a stable boundary that can become a pod charter.

The principle isn’t “make every team smaller.” It is: make ownership as small and as clear as the problem allows.

If a problem cannot be cleanly separated, don’t force an artificial boundary. But if a problem can be owned end to end by a small group, don’t add organizational complexity simply because more people are available.

Measure leverage, not activity

Traditional engineering metrics often measure activity: tickets completed, projects delivered, story points, utilization. Small pods need measures that make their leverage visible to the business.

I look for three categories.

Capacity

  • Scope owned per engineer
  • System scale supported per engineer
  • Operational load per engineer

These numbers reveal how much meaningful scope the organization can sustainably own.

Velocity

  • Lead time from request to production
  • Decision latency
  • Time spent waiting on another team

These show whether ownership is actually reducing organizational friction.

Leverage

  • Toil eliminated
  • Manual workflows automated
  • Systems retired
  • Capacity reclaimed
  • Recurring operational work eliminated

These capture the work that no longer requires human effort.

These are signals, not quotas. The goal is not to maximize scope per engineer, but to understand whether organizational leverage is increasing sustainably.

A small pod’s most valuable work is often invisible: an incident that never happened, a system that no longer exists, a manual process that no longer requires an engineer, a dependency that disappeared, a class of requests that became self-service.

If you don’t count those outcomes, the organization’s highest-leverage work becomes invisible. And invisible work does not survive budget season.

The real trade

None of this is a shortcut. Small pods demand sharper charters, stronger technical foundations, more discipline about leverage, and harder leadership decisions than large teams do.

That is the trade. You exchange the comfort of headcount for the compounding leverage of a few people who own something completely and multiply themselves through automation, platforms, AI and organizational clarity.

The goal isn’t fewer engineers. It is less organizational complexity per engineer.

The organizations that consistently deliver more aren’t necessarily the ones with the most people. They are the ones where small groups can own increasingly large scopes because the organization systematically removes coordination, toil and work that doesn’t require human judgment.

Scale the scope, not the team.

item.title: The impending tech economic crisis: Who’s going to pay for all this?
item.description:
There is a fundamental problem hiding behind today’s technology forecasts: the technology industry is projecting spending growth at rates that many of its customers cannot economically sustain.

Gartner’s July 2026 forecast calls for worldwide IT spending to increase 14.2% in 2026 to $6.37 trillion. Within that number, software is projected to rise 15.5%, Infrastructure-as-a-Service 29.3%, and data-center systems an extraordinary 62.5%. Gartner itself acknowledges that technology budgets are being strained by inflation, supply shortages, hardware and memory costs, and AI investment.

The AI projections are even more dramatic. Gartner’s September forecast puts 2026 worldwide AI spending at $2.7 trillion—up 49.5% in a single year. McKinsey has separately estimated that generative AI alone could drive $175–$250 billion of software spending by 2027, adding two to six percentage points to software-sector growth.

These are extraordinary numbers. But they expose a fundamental flaw in the way the technology market is being viewed: The forecasts measure what the technology industry expects to sell—not necessarily what its customers can afford to buy.

That distinction is critical.

The forecasts may describe what technology suppliers want to sell, what hyperscalers intend to build, and what analysts believe enterprises will demand. They do not demonstrate that the typical enterprise has the economic capacity to increase its technology budget at anything approaching those rates.

Dr. Howard A. Rubin

That is the collision illustrated in this cartoon. Most companies cannot indefinitely grow technology spending at 10%, 15%, 20%, 30% or even 50% when their revenues, operating margins and the economies in which they operate are growing at only a fraction of those rates.

And the affordability problem is actually worse than the headline spending forecasts suggest.

Enterprises simultaneously face the economic headwinds: IT inflation; AI premiums; rising compute, server and memory costs; cybersecurity; energy and datacenter requirements; technical debt; scarce technology talent; software and cloud price escalation; regulatory and control costs; and the continuing expense of maintaining yesterday’s technology while financing tomorrow’s.

The result is what I call the Technology Affordability Gap: Technology demand + technology inflation + AI investment + infrastructure requirements are growing faster than the economic capacity of many enterprises to pay for them.

This produces an extraordinary paradox. Every technology forecast can appear individually plausible from the supplier’s side while their collective implications become economically implausible from the customer’s side.

A hyperscaler can forecast enormous cloud growth. An AI company can forecast enormous AI adoption. A software company can forecast higher subscription revenue. A semiconductor company can forecast explosive demand for AI infrastructure. An analyst can add all of those expectations together.

But ultimately there is only one customer balance sheet paying the bills.

Something, therefore, has to give.

Enterprises will have to slow spending, eliminate legacy costs, consolidate vendors, renegotiate contracts, defer lower-value projects, substitute AI and automation for labor, radically improve technology productivity, and demand demonstrable economic returns from AI and other technology investments. Otherwise, technology spending will increasingly have to be financed by taking money away from other parts of the enterprise— or by sacrificing margins.

That is the impending Technology Economic Crisis.

It is not a crisis caused by a shortage of technology. It is potentially a crisis caused by more technology ambition, more technology supply and more technology spending expectations than the underlying economy can afford.

The question for 2027 and beyond, therefore, isn’t simply: “How much technology will companies want?”

It is: “How much technology can they actually afford?”

item.title: How CIOs can retain control as AI writes more code
item.description:
AI is writing more code than ever. Software specialist Sonar’s 2026 State of Code Developer Survey, based on more than 1,100 professional developers, found that 72% of those who’ve tried AI coding tools now use them every day, and that today, AI now accounts for 42% of committed code, a number that’s expected to reach 65% by next year.

But while developers embrace AI-enabled coding services, many professionals are uncertain about how their businesses will cope with this influx of AI-generated code. Sonar’s research additionally discovered that 96% of developers don’t fully trust it, and only 48% always verify it before committing.

In fact, 38% of developers told the researchers that reviewing AI code requires more effort than analyzing code written by human colleagues. That’s a pattern recognized by Tim Chilton, a managing geospatial consultant at UK mapping agency Ordnance Survey (OS). “There’s truth in the headlines that AI can get carried away, and developers spend more time fixing the code that’s been created than not,” he says.

While that’s not a pattern he sees at the OS, Chilton says his organization is cautious about how developers use AI coding tools, and conversations with other digital leaders suggest a similar approach. AI-enabled coding is indeed almost ubiquitous, and it can allow developers to reach new, higher levels of productivity, but more doesn’t necessarily mean better code.

To ensure that such coding services produce business benefits, CIOs must take control of the development process. They should exploit agents carefully, set professional responsibilities, and establish guidelines, policies, and organization-wide training.

Exploiting the agents

Snowflake co-founder and president Benoît Dageville suggests there are two ways to view AI-powered coding. One is the scary way, where AI takes over your tasks without human input. The second is the efficient way, where AI helps you do the same things as before, but at a fraction of the cost. He’s a big believer in the latter, both for himself and his teams.

“The route depends on the organization; their application of AI coding depends on their priorities,” he says. “However, I hope that overall, AI will have a positive effect on humans. I’m using AI every day to code, and if I compare myself to one or two years ago versus now, I’m more efficient and productive, but I’m also writing five times more code.”

Steve Lucas, CEO of integration technology specialist Boomi, also notes the increase in output. He quotes research that suggests 4% of GitHub public commits are already being authored by Claude Code. That proportion is expected to rise to 20% of all daily commits by the end of this year. Staff at Boomi already use AI tools to produce more code.

“We’re writing 10 times the amount today than we did two years ago,” says Lucas. The increase in AI-enabled coding is so significant that he’s spoken with Boomi chief product and technology officer Ed Macosky about goals for the proportion of self-modifying code.

“I believe AI should recursively modify 80% of a software organization’s code,” Macosky says. “Infinite improvement is demanded. If AI is extraordinarily good at breaking security protocols, the only way to keep up isn’t the kind of accordion model of human code design. AI use must be linear in scale and continuous.”

Crucially, Lucas suggests using AI to check and modify that AI doesn’t mean coders go away. “In fact, I think we’ll need more engineers, not fewer,” he says. “We need these professional experts to ensure the quality of the code that’s written.”

At OS, Chilton uses Coco, Snowflake’s coding agent. The tool does as much as 90% of a development task that he would otherwise complete from scratch. “It’s taken an hour to finish, instead of weeks or never,” he says, reflecting on the power of AI coding services.

However, the tool’s influence is carefully constrained. The agent doesn’t work in isolation, and Chilton checks its output in detail. He says all organizations need a similar process and should value experienced professionals who can use AI coding tools effectively.

“If you’re giving a tool to someone who isn’t capable of checking an agent’s work, as a digital leader, you run the risk of putting too much faith in AI just running with its output,” he says. “I think that’s a big risk, so there’s still a need for experienced developers.” 

Setting clear responsibilities

While placing humans in the loop can help ensure AI-enabled code is safe and effective, developers shouldn’t be weighed down by their new management responsibilities.

Gill Haus, CIO at Chase, the consumer banking arm of JPMorgan Chase & Co, says AI coding benefits can only be realized when agents are introduced with a strong focus on automating supporting technology and processes, which reduces the need for too much human input.

“If you have 12,000 engineers, they can write 12,000 engineers’ worth of code in a day,” he says. “If those 12,000 engineers have agentic technology, they can write much more. But if you don’t have automation left to right with confidence, you create more manual processes. You can’t move as quickly since there are only so many humans you can put in the middle.”

Haus says Chase never releases services in production that don’t pass its high bar for quality and security. Strong engineering practices, pipelines, and architecture, plus a tried-and-tested approach to automation, can help ensure AI coding produces solid outputs without a burdensome amount of human intervention.

“We’re focused on effective automation so we’re able to unleash this technology safely and effectively,” he says. “This is something many other companies should be focused on if they aren’t already, because otherwise you can’t keep up with the pace of change.”

François-Xavier Pierrel, group chief data and ad tech officer at French TV network TF1, is another digital leader who says maintaining control as AI writes more code means keeping the human in the loop in a clearly defined manner. His team documents agentic processes using Atlassian project management and collaboration tools, such as Confluence.

Pierrel says policy management is crucial as the agentic transformation gathers pace. One key step is ensuring professionals who use agents conform to internal standards. Smart businesses set policies that state clearly when staff can explore an agent, delegate work to it, or release it in production.

“We don’t have hundreds of agents deployed yet,” he says. “But the moment you reach a certain level of volume, if you don’t have compliance and policies in place, AI becomes a critical mess, and then it can be disruptive in a negative way.”

Building strong foundations

Kirsty Roth, chief operating officer at content and technology specialist Thomson Reuters, agrees digital leaders must be proactive. Her firm’s explorations with models and agents suggest that AI can help with time-intensive coding processes, such as writing. This capability means her organization carefully considers the roles people fulfil.

“In the last 12 months, we’ve put lots of thought into where we’re seeing benefits,” she says. “It’s great AI can do some of the coding work, but what does that mean for people’s jobs? We used to have thousands of engineers. Do we now need more architects or product people?”

Roth refers to security. While cyber is always a priority for Thomson Reuters, the firm dedicates significant resources to controlling threats in the AI age. Developing high-level development and security skills requires a concerted effort. Yet Roth says ensuring people have the right skills to manage AI is in many ways a familiar IT trend.

“All this effort is no different than digital, cloud, mobile, social, or other big tech trends,” she says. “They all take several years to have an impact as the initial hype comes, and then you’ve got to work through the reality and think about how you upskill people for the new world.”

Crucially, coding is no longer the sole preserve of the software developer. AI coding tools make it much easier for non-IT professionals to vibe code applications. Tal Carmi, CIO at technology specialist WalkMe, says non-developers can create useful tools. However, effective outputs rely on a careful balance between enablement and guidance.

He adds that most of these employees don’t need in-depth capabilities, such as a database or a content delivery network. Instead, non-IT staff require a dedicated place to upload their products. WalkMe’s engineering specialists ask key questions to ensure their outputs are safe, considering credentials and potentially problematic packages.

“You need to add guardrails,” he says. “A lot of the work for in-house engineers is shifting from building to testing. The people who aren’t coders don’t necessarily have security in mind.”

The key takeaway, suggests Emmanuel Frenehard, chief digital officer at biopharmaceutical giant Sanofi, is that digital leaders must help professionals feel comfortable. Successful digital leaders ensure the business generates value from agents, and his firm is helping its staff, particularly its developers, to embrace these tools.

“I genuinely worry for professionals who don’t use AI to code, because in five years, they may not have jobs,” he says. “So we’re guiding, coaching, and training them, but people must take the journey. The train has left the station. You can decide to be on it, or just look at it.”

item.title: Amazon ECS Gateway Arrives with Generated Hostnames and No Custom Domain Support
item.description:
AWS has released Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level ingress resource letting platform teams define networking once and application teams opt services in with a connector. Each service gets a generated hostname and routing is host-based, and neither the announcement nor the documentation covers custom domains.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Planning for the long game when technology has a shorter shelf life
item.description:
Over many years of working through successive waves of enterprise technology and IT architecture, including fast-moving AI, I’ve heard the same question in different forms: “How can I build my business with AI while avoiding lock-in and tech debt?”

It came up again during a recent conversation about a major technology investment, when a CIO asked, “Should we really be making this commitment if the technology is changing constantly?” That resonated with me because it reflects a pattern I have seen across technology waves: the architecture must provide stability even as the capabilities around it continue to evolve.

For decades, the goal has been to build a technology foundation that serves the enterprise for five, seven or even 10 years. With the emergence of AI, some technologies become outdated before implementation is complete.

If shorter technology lifecycles are the challenge, adaptability is the answer. Instead of asking, “What will serve us for the next decade?” CIOs should ask, “How can we remain flexible as technology changes?” That requires being deliberate about what must remain durable and where the enterprise must be ready to adapt.

Think of it like a house. The foundation, walls and furnace are built to last, while paint, furniture and bathrooms change as needs and styles evolve. Enterprise architecture increasingly works the same way.

AI is separating the experience of work from the systems behind it

I recently heard about a company that now gives new employees a single onboarding tool: ChatGPT, connected to the enterprise systems and key data sources behind it. Instead of learning multiple applications, employees simply ask for the information or support they need, without knowing which underlying system provides it.

Of course, a single interface doesn’t mean blanket access to enterprise systems. This model requires security measures that ensure employees can access only the information and capabilities they’re authorized to use: carrying each employee’s identity and existing permissions through every request, limiting access to what’s necessary, tracking where information comes from, and logging retrievals and actions. Changes with significant business consequences should also require review.

This does change how we think about work and the technology that supports it. If agents are becoming the primary interface, the central question shifts from “Which application should employees use?” to “Can our data be accessed, understood and used securely by the interfaces and agents we adopt next?”

Adaptability means running at two speeds

Some technology capabilities should endure; others should evolve quickly. The mistake is treating everything as having the same lifecycle.

The durable layer includes ERP, HCM and other core systems, along with data, security and foundational architecture. These investments remain essential, but CIOs should design them around future business possibilities rather than solely around today’s processes.

The fast-moving layer comprises agents, interfaces, analytics, workflows, AI models and tools, experiments and business-specific solutions. The CIO’s role is to distinguish this layer from the durable core and ensure that rapidly evolving capabilities can be replaced without destabilizing the durable foundation.

CIOs need practical ways to change the underlying technology without disrupting the applications the business relies on. That starts with clear, consistent rules for how systems exchange data and interact with APIs, MCP connections and AI agents, keeping the implementation choices behind those boundaries. Before changing a model, agent or application, teams should confirm existing data and integrations will keep working, test security and expected behavior, and introduce changes in stages with a rollback plan if something goes wrong.

This two-speed model is a substantial departure from traditional enterprise IT management and from the way we did things when I was coming up in the tech world. It changes how CIOs plan investments, organize technology functions, structure vendor relationships and govern the connections between durable and fast-moving capabilities.

Invest thoughtfully for both durability and adaptability

In the pre-AI era, CIOs prioritized technologies with decade-long relevance. Today, they should avoid overspending on solutions prone to rapid obsolescence and invest in business outcomes and a durable foundation for intelligence.

Projects lasting more than six months warrant scrutiny: Will the solution remain relevant, or are we embedding processes that AI may soon handle; perhaps with a single prompt?

Durability extends beyond core systems to include the organization’s capacity to understand, evaluate and adopt new technology.

Today, most companies critically underinvest in skills. Knowing how to operate ChatGPT or Claude is not the same as working effectively with AI. OpenAI’s study found that AI power users outperform average users by sixfold. Upskilling gives CIOs leverage by helping employees redesign work and use AI effectively, while stronger leadership fluency facilitates new business models rather than merely supporting existing operations.

Most companies are also underinvesting in the data foundation. In West Monroe’s recent survey of 417 business leaders, AI governance, risk and compliance ranked as the lowest investment priority for the next 12 months. Traditionally, IT addressed data operations to ensure successful ERP implementation. Now, because data quality directly impacts AI value, investing in governance and accessibility is imperative.

CIOs need practices that preserve data meaning and reliability as platforms change. Those include assigning clear ownership, establishing authoritative sources and shared definitions, tracking data lineage and setting standards for quality and access. Definitions and rules should be maintained in portable documentation and data contracts, rather than embedding them in a single AI model or vendor platform, so they carry forward as technology evolves.

Break down IT silos to encourage adaptive architecture

Typically, CIOs organize operations around disciplines such as infrastructure, data, applications and security, with IT teams choosing an application and then defining processes and architecture around it. But as future architecture becomes less certain, CIOs must instead envision future business capabilities and design for change, bringing AI and data into architectural thinking alongside traditional cloud and application expertise.

Consider a reporting process that today moves from data analysis to Excel to PowerPoint to human review before a decision is made. An adaptive architecture focuses less on preserving each of those steps and more on the outcome: turning data into intelligence that informs a decision or action. Excel and PowerPoint may still have a role, but they no longer need to be hardwired into the process.

CIOs also need to break down silos. Teams often define architecture around a single suite, such as Salesforce or SAP, without considering alternatives. While working with an energy company recently, I saw how bringing analytics teams into the discussion shifted the focus from the ERP itself to how data should be accessed and used. Small, cross-functional teams can help create that broader view and design around business needs rather than individual platforms.

Build partnerships around future business outcomes

The most effective CIOs I work with are shifting their focus from simply controlling costs to driving value, actively partnering with the business, and reimagining how functions can evolve with AI, data and IT.

As vendor offerings expand across applications, analytics, agents and interfaces, CIOs need to balance integrated ecosystems with the flexibility to combine providers. Prioritizing open standards, multi-cloud support, data portability, interoperability and adaptable contracts can help organizations use the strongest elements of core systems while integrating agents and data across systems to adapt faster as needs evolve.

CIOs should build flexibility into vendor contracts, so changing providers doesn’t mean losing access to valuable data, context or governance rules. Contracts should provide for usable exports of data and metadata, documented interfaces that vendors keep current, advance notice of discontinued features, and support for testing portability and transitioning to another provider. They should also specify security and audit obligations throughout the relationship and during the transition.

The bottom line: buy with the future in mind. Don’t just ask if an application meets current requirements. Instead, envision what future business functions should look like, then derive technology needs from that vision. Shift the mindset from using HCM checklists to driving workforce optimization, from CRM checklists to revenue management, and from ERP checklists to enterprise data and intelligence.

Find the signal in the noise

As AI gets smarter and cheaper, the challenge will shift from affording it to connecting it to business outcomes. I believe the defining constraint in 2027 will be focus, not cost: CIOs must identify the few high-leverage priorities their organizations can absorb and execute well. That’s easier said than done.

There’s no established playbook for the AI era: we’re all experiencing it for the first time. CIOs face a flood of startups, models, architectural approaches, evolving standards, vendor claims and internal requests. The task becomes curation: deciding what deserves attention. Distinguishing signal from noise is becoming an essential leadership skill.

The new long game for CIOs

I believe CIOs are at a pivotal moment. They can remain excellent IT leaders or help the business rethink work through intelligence. In that sense, the role could evolve into what I call the chief intelligence officer: the leader who helps the enterprise turn fast-changing technology into durable business value.

item.title: Journify Raises $12M Series A Amid 5x Growth
item.description:
Investors back Journify’s push into the US and Europe

Journify, the ad signal infrastructure company, today announced a $12 million Series A at four times its previous valuation. Al Mada Ventures led the round, co-led by returning investor Silicon Badia, with Shorooq and Bunat Ventures increasing their investment and Du Ventures and Oraseya Capital joining as new investors. The funding will take Journify into the US and Europe and expand the AI behind its platform.

Global ad spend will exceed $1 trillion in 2026, with algorithms expected to place three quarters by 2028, according to dentsu. These systems learn from the customer outcomes brands send back. Browser restrictions, broken tracking, and disconnected offline sales leave them with an incomplete picture of who buys.

Journify makes sure ad platforms such as Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap and Amazon Ads see the purchases, sign-ups and store sales a brand’s customers actually make. More than 100 businesses use Journify today, from fast-growing ecommerce brands to some of the region’s largest retailers, representing hundreds of millions of dollars in annual ad spend.

Customers include Jarir Bookstore, one of Saudi Arabia’s largest retailers, which increased its return on ad spend on Meta by 182%, and Saudi ecommerce brand Baytonia, which grew its return on ad spend on TikTok by 80% while cutting cost per purchase by 44%.

“AI is transforming advertising, but the intelligence behind it is only as good as the signals it receives,” said Taoufik El Jamali, Co-Founder and CEO of Journify. “Businesses know who buys, who comes back and what creates lasting customer value. Too little of that knowledge reaches the ad platforms driving their growth. Our vision is to close that gap, turning real customer outcomes into intelligence ad platforms can learn from. We’re building toward a future where advertising AI understands what makes a customer valuable to each business, not just what makes them click.”“As AI takes on a greater role in marketing, we believe the connection between reliable customer data and the decisions built on it will become increasingly valuable,” said Omar Laalej, Managing Director at Al Mada Ventures. “What interests us about Journify is its approach to building that connection from the data layer up: a privacy-first foundation that can evolve into intelligence and action. The founders’ understanding of that opportunity gives us confidence in their ability to build a platform that marketers can increasingly rely on, both to understand their customers and to act on that understanding.”Hossam Shafick, Partner at Silicon Badia, Seed Lead and returning investor, added, “Since our initial investment, Journify has grown its valuation by more than 4x, and its revenues more than 5x, validating both the strength of its technology and the team’s ability to execute at scale. That performance has deepened our conviction that Journify can become a global leader in ad signal infrastructure. We are proud to double down and co-lead this round as the company expands into the world’s largest advertising markets.”

Journify already uses AI to monitor every connection continuously, detect signal-quality issues and fix them. The new funding will grow those capabilities as Journify expands beyond the GCC. In the US alone, digital advertising revenue reached $294.6 billion in 2025, according to IAB and PwC.

“I’m excited to help Journify scale in the biggest ad market in the world,” said Ryan Burke, a newly appointed member of Journify’s board and three-time Chief Revenue Officer. “I’ve known Taoufik since our InVision days, and I’ve seen his product execution in action. Based on the success they’re already seeing in the Middle East, it’s not a question whether it works in the US, but how fast we can scale.”

About Journify

Journify builds ad signal infrastructure for performance marketers. Its privacy-first, real-time data layer helps brands improve the quality and reliability of the first-party signals used in advertising and measurement.

Journify connects data across web, mobile, offline sales, CRM, ecommerce platforms, backend systems and data warehouses. It validates and enriches conversion events and activates consented signals server-side across Google, Meta, TikTok, Snap, Amazon Ads and other platforms.

Founded in 2022 by Taoufik El Jamali, Amine Chouki and Omar Al Shoubaki, Journify is headquartered in San Francisco with offices in Dubai and Riyadh. Learn more at journify.io.

Journify has obtained a SOC 2 Type II report and is committed to GDPR compliance.
